elements.id-string-3: How to detect and mitigate deceptive AI systems is an open problem for the field of safe and trustworthy AI.
elements.id-string-4: We analyse two algorithms for mitigating deception:The first is based on the path-specific objectives framework where paths in the game that incentivise deception are removed.The second is based on shielding, i.e., monitoring for unsafe policies and replacing them with a safe reference policy.We construct two simple games and evaluate our algorithms empirically.We find that both methods ensure that our agent is not deceptive, however, shielding tends to achieve higher reward.
elements.id-string-6: Deception is a challenge for building safe and trustworthy AI \cite{me}.
elements.id-string-7: Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) and language models (LMs) mean that we are increasingly living in a world containing highly capable, goal-directed \emph{agents} \cite{gpt4technicalreport2023}.
elements.id-string-8: Deception may be learned as an effective strategy for achieving goals in many environments, especially in multi-agent settings comprised of humans and AI agents \cite{me}.
elements.id-string-9: Technical work on deception in AI systems, and how to avoid it, is limited.
elements.id-string-10: Deception has been defined within structural causal games (SCGs), which is a framework that applies causal graphs to game theory \cite{me}.
elements.id-string-11: Given a causal graph, it is possible to ensure certain safety properties by removing paths in that causal graph \cite{Farquhar2022Jun}.
elements.id-string-12: Giving learning agents these kinds of \emph{path-specific objectives} (PSOs) is also applicable when deception is the property that is considered unsafe.
elements.id-string-13: These methods ensure that the agent will not deceive a human providing feedback, however, it will also ensure that the agent will not persuade, teach, or coordinate with the human (i.e., it will not try to influence the human in any way).
elements.id-string-14: Shielding is another class of methods for ensuring safety in learning agents \cite{OdriozolaOlaldeZA23, carr2023safe, waga2022dynamic, KonighoferBEP22, Elsayed-AlyBAET21, giacobbe2021shielding, AlshiekhBEKNT18}.
elements.id-string-15: A shield is a kind of monitor.
elements.id-string-16: In addition to monitoring, the shield replaces an unsafe action with a safe action if the verification returns that the policy does not satisfy the safety specification.

elements.id-string-25: \textbf{Structural Causal Games (SCGs)} offer a representation of causality in games \cite{Hammond}.
elements.id-string-26: An SCG is a directed acyclic graph containing variables and causal edges between them.
elements.id-string-27: There are three types of variables: chance variables ($X$), decision variables ($D$) and utility variables ($U$).
elements.id-string-28: Along with the graph, an SCG defines the conditional probability distribution (CPD) over each (non-decision) variable, given its parents.
elements.id-string-29: Agent's policies choose the CPD over decision variables and agents choose their policies to maximise the expected sum of utility and we use the Nash equilibrium concept.
elements.id-string-30: At the beginning of the game a \emph{setting} is sampled from the prior over the game; given a setting and a policy profile, the value of any variable is uniquely determined.
elements.id-string-31: Kenton et al. \cite{kenton2022discovering} define \emph{agents} in SCGs as systems that would adapt their policy if their actions influenced the world in a different way.
elements.id-string-32: This is the relevant notion of agency, as
elements.id-string-33: we define belief and intent based on how the agent would adapt its behaviour to such changes.

elements.id-string-139: \emph{Summary} We introduce a novel shielding algorithm for mitigating deceptive learning agents.
elements.id-string-140: We show, in two toy environments, that our algorithm has advantages over previous methods.
elements.id-string-141: \emph{Limitations and future work} The examples are simplistic, and the optimal policies are very easy to find analytically without doing any training.
elements.id-string-142: This work acts as a proof of concept for the idea of automatically detecting and preventing deception while training.
elements.id-string-143: Many simplifying assumptions are made, e.g. the fact that the games only have one time-step, or the assumption that one of the policies is fixed.
elements.id-string-144: In addition, the verification is exhaustive on the setting space.
elements.id-string-145: This works with the small domains of these examples but might become intractable for larger and more realistic problems, which could require Monte-Carlo sampling of the setting, or a latent representation of it.
elements.id-string-146: Furthermore, shielding requires an initial safe reference policy, and its convergence to good safe policies is unknown.
